COVID Coffers - How to spend R500 billion

By: Siniketiwe Hlanze | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As the country amends its budget and looks to take up billions of loans to reconfigure the economy is this the right strategy to help South Africa survive COVID-19

Unique Selling Point:
Whilst South Africa's health and humanitarian response to COVID 19 response has been lauded around the world, its efforts to save the economy will test its resilience to survive the pandemic. Global financial institutions have made available relief loan facilities to countries at a lower interest rate with minimal conditions. The loans government officials are considering will be channeled for both health efforts and economic stimulus a move that raises concerns about the added debt burden on an already constrained fiscus, a legacy of stringent loan conditions especially on poor countries, corruption and the recovery of the economy.

Summary:
Treasury DG, Dondo Mogojane, says the country is looking to borrow about R95 billion from global financial institutions as part of the country's R500 billion relief package. The primary condition for these loans is that they be used for COVID 19 projects only. An interview with a treasury representative will unpack details of the interest rates, conditions and payment terms of the loans. Economist Dr Sean Muller will provide commentary on how the loans will impact South Africa's fiscal position, how soon we'll have to borrow again once the COVID wave has passed and are there alternatives that don't involve borrowing. New Development (Brics) Director General for South Africa, Ratsoma Monale will talk about the loan offering they are providing and conditions there of. World Bank representative (not yet confirmed) will provide the same for their organisation.

As economic activity resumes albeit under limited measures under level 4 lockdown, an interview with a printing and packaging factory owner, on sight, will illustrate what the 'new normal' for business and economy looks like and how South Africa's economic relief efforts are important to keep industry afloat and people employed. These visuals will also illustrate the discussion about how South Africa is going to reimagine an economy that is highly dependent on labour.

Further information:
We've learnt corruption at all spheres of governance will creep in especially if there are funds released for urgent projects.The Auditor General's office say they are having to think strategically about how to make sure that the monies released for COVID relief are used for the appropriate projects and are not embazzled. They are currently in discussions with Treasury and other stakeholders about what this plan will look like.

Script:


BOXING LINK:
Imagine South Africa’s economy just a couple of weeks ago, battered, no growth and sluggish. Then an outbreak of the CORONA virus brought with it more challenges, job losses, a health crisis, businesses shutting down, a humanitarian crisis, a shrinking GDP……we are in for some tough times -


VO: A hustle to claw back the remnants of an economy ravaged by a harsh lockdown.

While South Africa has been commended for its health response to COVID-19, now in sharp focus is how it will deal with the economic fallout.

VO: A 500 billion package was announced to mitigate the free fall of the economy, and to bolster the health and social response.
VO: economically, it’s designed to offer a lifeline to businesses and industry and to help prevent job losses


07:13 Tommy – we’ve asked staff to stay at home, and eh no-work no-pay rule applies however we’re trying to rotate them all the time with other stuff so they get a chance to come into work and earn some money
VO: Tommy Du Sart owns a printing and labelling factory in downtown Johannesburg.

For weeks now the printing plant has been virtually empty, a 90 percent decrease in orders means there simply isn’t enough work coming in to continue operating. The lull is used for machine maintenance.


11:30 Tommy – The calls we get “that we wanna come back to work please” “there’s no food” , it’s heartbreaking. This is the worst ever, we’ve been through recessions, we’ve been through a lot in the last 30 years. It’s never been as bad as this..
07:41 Derek – How do you see the future or the next year ahead
07:45 Tommy- (looking despondent) well eh Derek it’s hard to tell, if the lockdown lifts I think we can recover pretty quickly. You know printing depends on all other industries, without all other industries working, we wont get any printing so it’s all sort of linked together, yes it’s hard to tell.


LINK – Whilst the easing of lockdown is bringing much needed reprieve to some industries they may never catch up to the weeks of lost productivity. The factory floor is not as busy as it used be, so much is on the line for the people that work here

VO: The R500 billion package will come from an adjusted budget, government guarantees and about R95 billion sourced from international financial institutions.


Link: As a member state of the World Bank, IMF and New Development South Africa is eligible for the emergency relief funds from both these institutions




VO: And while the IMF and World Bank have emphasised that COVID-19 relief funds will be released faster, at a lower than usual interest rate and without conditionalities...some quarters believe that South Africa should cautiously read the fine print before signing on the dotted line.


02:00 people are afraid that they will then dictate to South Africa what our policy should be
VO: Busi Sibeko is an economist and researcher at the Institute for Economic Justice


Busi 00:50 those institutions have given a lot of financing and aid to a lot of African countries and in particular a lot developing countries and these have not yielded the kind of structural reforms and structural transformations that they were anticipated
She claims there are more strategic avenues to raise funds here at home


04:15 we can explore non conventional tools that we haven’t done in the past. Even with what SARB is doing now is unprecedented in our country they are doing more than what we usually see.
VO: Created by the BRICS Nations to finance infrastructure projects - and now in the wake of the COVID-19 crisis - The New Development Bank is reconfiguring its mandate.
Director General, Ratsoma Monale says negotiations for a 1 billion dollar loan are at an advanced stage.



4:33 – we have obviously had to make a few exceptions to our traditional way of doing business, in this case you are responding to a crisis, it so goes then that you need to respond swiftly
05:11 And quite important aspect of the loan is that it will have a grace period, then the borrower doesn’t have to pay back from day1.


13:14 Derek – It does seem that covd 19 will be with us for a while can countries apply for another loan later
13:21 Ratsoma – It is likely, already there’s eh we are starting to think about what the next phase of the economic response will be.

19:58 Ratsoma – I think eh consequences, consequence is too strong a word in this instance. We’re not the first in the business of loans and if there was to be a renegotiation or a default we would also not be the first institution to experience such it has happened time and time and across the globe. And there are processes to negotiate those. And in this case we are talking about an extreme event, South Africa is a 20percent shareholder in the bank and therefore it makes for easier conversation between the management of the bank and the shareholder. I don’t foresee that risk materialising
MANDELA BRIDGE LINK:
A revised budget, relief package and multilateral loans, can these resuscitate an economy that remains on life support -

VO: We’re yet to see the true reflection of the damage that COVID-19 has done to the economy. But . But experts warn that the GDP will shrink further that the will shrink further and we will see the worst economic decline centuryin a century.
With the first signs of an economic recovery expected only in 2021, Dr Shaun Muller, economist at the University of Johannesburg says South Africa is still in the eye of the storm




14:08 Derek – Essentially the economic response that we’re talking about is it more of a relief or a stimulus
14:14 Shaun – It’s definitely more of a relief, and I think that’s appropriate. I think framing the economic response of government as being about stimulus isn’t right.
18:04 Shaun – I think rebuilding the economy is only going to happen once we’ve gotten through the crisis. And at this point it’s not clear to me and I don’t think it’s clear to the government when that will be. SO at this point it is a crisis, so we’re tying to stem the building so until we are done with that it really doesn’t make sense to talk about getting us back on our feet and into athletic shape
I can tell you right now that South Africa is not in any position to have a fiscal stimulus anytime in the near future.


VO: For economist and member of the planning commission, Dr Miriam Altman, an economic recovery can only be possible once the lockdown regulations allow for more businesses to operate



22:41 Miriam So the first thing to get us to growth is that you don’t have so much business failure, the second thing is to get us to IRP, you know the energy investments, get more home building and urban development and transport and all of those things kinds of investments that create jobs
